8000: Humidity is the amount of water vapor present in the air. Water vapor is simply water in its invisible, gaseous form — not droplets, not rain, just water molecules floating freely in the air around you.
Think of the air as a sponge. Just like a sponge can soak up water, air can "hold" water vapor. Humidity is a measure of how much water that sponge (the air) is currently holding.
Why does air hold water vapor at all?

Water from oceans, lakes, rivers, wet soil, and even plants constantly evaporates — it turns into invisible vapor and rises into the air. That vapor stays suspended in the atmosphere. The amount of vapor present at any given time and place is what we call humidity.
The three main forms of humidity

There are three precise ways scientists and meteorologists express humidity, and understanding all three gives you the complete picture.

1. Absolute Humidity

This is the simplest form. It tells you the actual mass of water vapor contained in a specific volume of air — usually measured in grams per cubic metre (g/m³). If a cubic metre of air holds 15 grams of water vapor, its absolute humidity is 15 g/m³. It's a raw, direct count with no comparisons involved.

2. Relative Humidity

This is the form you encounter most in daily life — weather forecasts, air conditioner displays, and news reports all use this. It is expressed as a percentage (%).

Relative humidity tells you how close the air is to being completely full of water vapor. Specifically, it is the ratio of the amount of water vapor actually present in the air to the maximum amount that air could possibly hold at that temperature.

Relative humidity (%) = (actual water vapor ÷ maximum possible water vapor) × 100

So if the relative humidity is 50%, the air is holding exactly half the water vapor it is capable of holding at that temperature. If it is 100%, the air is completely saturated — it cannot accept even one more molecule of water vapor. At that point, water vapor begins to condense into tiny liquid droplets, forming clouds, fog, dew, or rain.

3. Specific Humidity

This is used mainly in meteorology and atmospheric science. It measures the mass of water vapor per unit mass of the total air (including the vapor itself), expressed in grams per kilogram (g/kg). It is more precise than absolute humidity for atmospheric calculations because it doesn't change when air is compressed or expanded (unlike absolute humidity, which is volume-dependent). For everyday understanding, this form matters less than the first two.
The critical link between temperature and humidity

This is one of the most important things to understand about humidity: warm air can hold significantly more water vapor than cold air.

Imagine a small glass and a large glass. The large glass can hold more water before overflowing. In the same way, warm air has a higher capacity for water vapor than cold air.

This has a fascinating consequence for relative humidity:

  • If you take a parcel of air and heat it, its capacity for water vapor increases — so even if the actual amount of vapor stays the same, the relative humidity falls, because the air is now "less full."
  • If you take the same air and cool it, its capacity shrinks — so the relative humidity rises, because the same amount of vapor now occupies a larger fraction of the smaller capacity.

This is exactly why it often feels more humid at night: the temperature drops, the air's capacity shrinks, and the relative humidity climbs — even though no new water vapor has entered the air.

Closely related to humidity is the concept of the dew point. This is the specific temperature to which air must be cooled (without changing its pressure or actual water vapor content) before it becomes completely saturated — reaching 100% relative humidity. Any further cooling beyond the dew point causes water vapor to condense into liquid: you see it as dew on grass in the morning, fog in a valley, or water droplets on a cold glass on a warm day. The higher the dew point, the more moisture is actually in the air, making it feel "heavier" and muggier.
How humidity affects your daily life

High humidity (say, above 70%) makes hot days feel even hotter and more uncomfortable. This happens because your body cools itself by sweating — sweat evaporates off your skin, carrying heat away with it. But when the air is already packed with water vapor, sweat evaporates slowly or barely at all. Your body can't shed heat efficiently, so you feel hotter and more oppressive than the temperature alone would suggest. This combined effect is captured in the heat index (also called "feels like" temperature). High humidity also encourages mold, mildew, rust, and bacteria growth; causes wood and paper to swell; and makes surfaces feel clammy or damp.

Low humidity (say, below 30%) has its own problems. Dry air pulls moisture out of anything it contacts — your skin, your lips, your throat, and your nasal passages. This leads to chapped lips, dry skin, nosebleeds, sore throats, and an increased susceptibility to respiratory infections (because the mucous membranes that trap germs dry out). Low humidity also causes wood to shrink and crack (furniture, flooring, musical instruments), creates static electricity, and can make contact lenses uncomfortable.

Comfortable humidity for humans is generally considered to be between 30% and 60% relative humidity. Most air conditioners, heaters, humidifiers, and dehumidifiers are designed to keep indoor air within this range.

Humidity is at the heart of how weather works. Water vapor in the air carries energy (called latent heat). When that vapor condenses into clouds and rain, it releases that energy, which powers storms, winds, and weather systems. Tropical regions near the equator tend to have very high humidity because the intense heat constantly evaporates water from the ocean. Deserts, on the other hand, have extremely low humidity because there is little water to evaporate and the heat quickly dissipates any vapor that forms.

Humidity is the presence of water vapor in the air. Relative humidity — the most everyday form — tells you, as a percentage, how saturated the air is with that vapor compared to how much it could theoretically hold. Warm air holds more; cool air holds less. Too much humidity makes heat unbearable and encourages dampness and mold; too little dries everything out. Clouds, rain, dew, and fog are all humidity reaching its tipping point.
8001:
To humiliate someone means to make them feel deeply ashamed, embarrassed, and stripped of their dignity — to make them feel small, inferior, and powerless. It's one of the most emotionally painful things one person can do to another.

A helpful way to picture it: think of dignity as a kind of invisible armor every person wears — a sense of self-respect and worth. To humiliate someone is to rip that armor off, often in front of an audience, leaving them exposed, helpless, and ashamed.

"Humiliate" sits at the extreme end of a scale of embarrassment. Imagine it like this:

Embarrass → Shame → Humiliate

To embarrass someone is relatively mild — perhaps they tripped and people chuckled. To shame someone is more serious — they feel bad about what they did or who they are. To humiliate someone is the most painful of all — their dignity is crushed, often in front of others, and the wound can last a long time. Use this word only when the emotional damage is deep and significant.

Three things are almost always present when humiliation occurs:

A loss of dignity. The person is made to feel worthless, inferior, or beneath others. Their self-respect is damaged.

Serious, deep shame. This is far beyond ordinary embarrassment. It's a burning, heavy feeling — the kind that makes a person wish they could disappear.

A power element. The person doing the humiliating often has some kind of advantage — more status, more authority, more popularity, or simply the ability to control the moment. This power imbalance is what makes it feel so crushing.
Does It Always Happen in Public?

Not always — but the public dimension makes humiliation dramatically more painful. Being humiliated privately stings. Being humiliated in front of others — colleagues, classmates, a crowd — multiplies the pain because your shame is witnessed, your reputation is affected, and you feel judged by everyone present. This is why the most painful humiliations in life tend to be public ones.

Usually, yes. Most of the time, someone humiliates another person deliberately — they want to make that person feel small. However, humiliation can also be unintentional. A person can accidentally humiliate someone through carelessness or a lack of awareness.

  • Intentional: "The bully humiliated the new kid by reading his embarrassing diary out loud to the whole class."
  • Unintentional: "She didn't mean to humiliate him, but loudly correcting his mistake in front of his team had that effect."

Yes. You can be the cause of your own humiliation — meaning you did or said something that brought deep shame upon yourself.

  • "He humiliated himself by boasting loudly about his skills and then failing completely in front of everyone."

• "The general humiliated his soldiers by making them march in the rain as punishment for a small mistake."
  • "She was humiliated when her private diary was read aloud at the family dinner."
  • "The chess champion was humiliated by a twelve-year-old newcomer."
  • "He never forgave his boss for humiliating him in front of the entire department."
  • "The corrupt politician was humiliated when the evidence of his crimes was broadcast on live television."

These all belong to the same word family:

Humiliation (noun) — the act itself, or the feeling it produces. "It was the greatest humiliation of his career."

Humiliating (adjective) — used to describe an experience or act that causes humiliation. "It was a humiliating defeat."

Humiliated (adjective/past participle) — used to describe how a person feels as a result. "She felt completely humiliated."
Similar Words — and How They Differ

Understanding these nearby words will sharpen your understanding of "humiliate" itself.

Embarrass — mild and often accidental. Spilling coffee on yourself in public is embarrassing. Embarrassment fades quickly. Humiliation is far deeper and more lasting.

Shame — shame can be internal (you feel it yourself, about yourself), while humiliation is usually caused by something external — something done to you. You can feel shame alone in a room; humiliation is almost always tied to how others see you.

Demean — to treat someone as though they have no value or deserve no respect. It's close to humiliate, but "demean" focuses more on disrespect and belittling, while "humiliate" focuses on the crushing emotional experience of the victim.

Degrade — to lower someone's status or treat them in a way that strips away their humanity. Often used in more systematic or physical contexts, such as degrading treatment in a prison. It's slightly colder and more clinical than "humiliate."

Mortify — to cause extreme embarrassment, often from something trivial or accidental. ("She was mortified when she called her teacher 'mom' in front of everyone.") It's dramatic but usually less aggressive and deliberate than "humiliate."

To humiliate someone is to deliberately (or sometimes accidentally) destroy their sense of dignity and make them feel deeply ashamed — especially in front of others. It involves a loss of self-respect, a feeling of powerlessness, and often a public wound that is hard to forget. It is one of the strongest and most emotionally charged words in the English language for describing how one person can make another feel small.
8002:
When you describe something as humiliating, you mean that it causes a person to feel deeply ashamed, embarrassed, and stripped of their dignity — especially in front of other people. It makes you feel small, looked down upon, and worthless. It wounds your pride badly.

Think of it this way: if something embarrassing makes you blush, something humiliating makes you wish the ground would open up and swallow you whole.

The key idea behind this word is the loss of dignity. Dignity is the feeling that you deserve respect — from yourself and from others. When something is humiliating, it attacks that feeling directly. It makes you feel inferior, powerless, or exposed in a way that is painful.

This is why "humiliating" is a much stronger word than just "embarrassing." Something embarrassing is awkward or uncomfortable. Something humiliating goes deeper — it damages how you see yourself and how you feel others see you. It leaves a mark.

A situation, event, or experience is called humiliating when it:

  • Exposes your weakness, failure, or mistake — especially publicly
  • Makes you feel inferior or lesser than others
  • Strips away your sense of self-respect or pride
  • Leaves you feeling powerless or unable to defend yourself

The public element is very important. Humiliation is almost always made worse — or even created — by the presence of other people watching. Being scolded privately can sting. Being scolded in front of a room full of colleagues is humiliating.

That said, something can feel humiliating even in private — if it strikes deeply enough at your pride or self-worth.

Here are some situations people commonly describe as humiliating, to help you feel the word clearly:

A student walks to the front of the class to present their project, and their mind goes completely blank. They stand there in silence while thirty classmates stare. That is a humiliating experience.

A footballer misses an easy, open goal in front of thousands of fans, and the stadium groans. That is a humiliating moment.

A job applicant confidently gives a wrong answer to a very basic question during an interview, and the interviewer raises an eyebrow and shakes their head slowly. That feels humiliating.

A person trips and falls in the middle of a busy shopping street while everyone around them stops and watches. Humiliating.

In each case, notice the pattern: something goes wrong or is exposed, others witness it, and the person is left feeling small, ashamed, and stripped of their dignity.

Both words come from the same root, but they work differently in a sentence, and you must know the difference.

Humiliating describes the thing, event, or experience that causes the feeling. It answers the question: "What was it like?"
→ "It was a humiliating experience."
→ "That was a humiliating defeat."

Humiliated describes the person who feels the emotion. It answers the question: "How did you feel?"
→ "I felt completely humiliated."
→ "She looked humiliated."

Think of it like the word "frightening" vs. "frightened." The horror movie is frightening. You are frightened by it. Similarly, the situation is humiliating. You are humiliated by it.

"Humiliating" sits near the stronger end of the scale when it comes to shame and embarrassment. Here is a rough sense of the intensity ladder, from mild to severe:

Awkward → Embarrassing → Humiliating → Degrading / Mortifying

"Awkward" is just uncomfortable. "Embarrassing" is noticeably worse. "Humiliating" is deeply painful and targets your dignity specifically. "Degrading" and "mortifying" are close in strength to "humiliating," and all three are often used interchangeably in everyday speech.

Yes — and this is an important nuance.

Sometimes a situation is humiliating by accident. Nobody planned it; it just happened, and you ended up feeling small. Tripping in public is like this.

But other times, humiliation is deliberate. A person or group can intentionally try to humiliate someone — by mocking them, putting them down in public, exposing their secrets, or forcing them into a degrading situation. When humiliation is intentional, it carries an additional layer of cruelty, because someone chose to do that to another person.

Here are natural sentence patterns you will often encounter:

  • "That was a deeply humiliating moment for him."
  • "She found the whole experience utterly humiliating."
  • "They suffered a humiliating defeat — 7 goals to 0."
  • "It was humiliating to be corrected in front of everyone."
  • "He gave her a humiliating look, as if she were completely foolish."
  • "The team's performance was nothing short of humiliating."

Notice how "humiliating" is often strengthened by words like deeply, utterly, completely, or publicly — because speakers want to emphasize just how severe the loss of dignity was.

Since you are learning this word completely, here is every form of it you will meet:

Humiliate (verb) — the action: "He tried to humiliate her in front of the class."
Humiliation (noun) — the experience or feeling: "She never forgot the humiliation of that day."
Humiliated (adjective) — how the person feels: "He walked away feeling deeply humiliated."
Humiliating (adjective) — what the thing or situation is like: "It was a humiliating experience."
Humiliatingly (adverb) — how something happens: "They lost humiliatingly, in front of their home crowd."

If you need to remember just one thing: humiliating describes something that causes a deep loss of dignity and self-respect, leaving you feeling ashamed and small — especially when others are watching.
8003:
Humiliation is the painful experience of having your dignity taken away — of being made to feel small, worthless, or deeply inferior, usually by another person, a group, or a situation beyond your control.

To understand it fully, think about dignity first. Dignity is the quiet, inner sense that you matter — that you deserve basic respect as a human being. It is something every person naturally carries. Humiliation is a direct attack on that feeling. It does not just make you feel bad; it makes you feel reduced — as if your worth as a person has been publicly damaged or destroyed.
The two ways the word is used

"Humiliation" functions in two closely related ways:

As a feeling: It describes the painful emotion a person experiences after being degraded.
"She walked out of the room filled with humiliation."

As an act or event: It describes the situation or action that caused the feeling.
"Being fired in front of the whole office was a terrible humiliation."

In both uses, the idea is the same — dignity has been harmed.
What it actually feels like

When someone is humiliated, they typically experience a sudden, burning awareness that they have been exposed as inferior or inadequate. They feel powerless — they could not stop it from happening. There is often a desperate urge to disappear, hide, or escape. And beneath all of it sits a deep wound to their sense of self-worth.

Psychologists consider humiliation one of the most painful emotional experiences a human being can go through — more distressing than simple sadness or even anger, because it strikes at the very foundation of how a person sees themselves.
How it differs from embarrassment and shame

These three words are often confused, but each has its own distinct meaning.

Embarrassment is lighter and often accidental. If you trip and fall in public, you feel embarrassed — momentarily awkward and red-faced. But it passes quickly, and nobody deliberately caused it. Your worth as a person is not really under attack.

Shame is a deep, private feeling that you yourself are bad, broken, or not good enough. It lives inside you. You can feel shame completely alone, with no one watching at all.

Humiliation is different from both. It almost always involves something or someone external making you feel degraded — and critically, it carries a social and witnessed quality. While shame says "I am bad," humiliation says "I have been made to look worthless in front of others." That public exposure of your weakness or inferiority is what gives humiliation its unique, sharp sting. It is not just about how you feel about yourself — it is about your standing in the eyes of the world being damaged.
What causes it

Humiliation can come from many directions. Another person can cause it deliberately — a bully who mocks you in front of a crowd, a boss who belittles you in a meeting, a partner who disrespects you publicly. Circumstances can cause it accidentally — forgetting your lines on stage, failing badly in a very public way, having your private information exposed to others without your consent. Systems and institutions can cause it too — a government that degrades its own people, a school that punishes a student unfairly and publicly.

What all these situations share is this: something has stripped away your control, your dignity, or your status — and done so in a way that felt exposed.
The role of other people watching

The social dimension is one of the most defining features of humiliation. It almost always involves — or at least feels like it involves — other people witnessing your degradation. Even when something humiliating happens in private, the person often imagines how others would react if they knew. This imagined audience is enough to produce the feeling.

This is why public humiliation is considered especially devastating. The more people who witness your loss of dignity, the deeper the wound tends to be. A mistake made privately can be recovered from quietly; a mistake made in front of many people feels carved into your identity.
The power dynamic

Humiliation almost always involves an imbalance of power. The person being humiliated is placed in a position of weakness, while the person or force doing the humiliating holds the upper hand — at least in that moment. This is part of why humiliation feels so painful and so hard to shake: you were not just hurt, you were made to feel helpless while being hurt.
How severe can it be?

Humiliation exists on a wide spectrum. On the milder end, a teacher correcting you in front of the class might leave you feeling slightly reduced. In the middle, a manager criticising your work harshly in front of your colleagues can be deeply upsetting. At its most extreme — public shaming, being stripped of your reputation or status before a large audience, or being deliberately degraded in an ongoing, systematic way — humiliation can cause serious and lasting emotional damage, sometimes even contributing to trauma.
Singular vs. plural

"Humiliation" in the singular refers to the experience as a whole or to one specific incident. "Humiliations" in the plural refers to multiple separate incidents or acts.

"After years of small humiliations at that workplace, she finally quit."
Example sentences to cement your understanding

• "The public humiliation of being laughed off the stage stayed with him for years."
  • "She felt a wave of humiliation when her private letter was read aloud to the class."
  • "The team's 9–0 loss was a national humiliation."
  • "He smiled and said nothing, hiding the humiliation he felt inside."
  • "The prisoners were subjected to repeated humiliations designed to break their spirit."
The one-sentence summary

Humiliation is the experience of having your dignity stripped away — of being made to feel worthless, inferior, or powerless, especially in the eyes of others — and it is one of the most painful things a human being can go through.
8004:
Humility is the quality of having an accurate, grounded sense of your own importance — not inflated, not deflated, but realistic. A person with humility does not think they are better or more important than others. At the same time, they don't think they are worthless or inferior either. It is a calm, clear-eyed understanding of where you actually stand.

Think of it this way: humility is the middle ground between arrogance ("I am the greatest, I know best, I matter most") and self-pity ("I am nothing, I am useless, I don't matter at all"). A humble person sits comfortably in the truth.

This is where most people get confused, so this part is important.

Humility is not weakness. A humble person can be strong, confident, and decisive. In fact, some of the most capable and respected people in history were deeply humble. Humility doesn't shrink you — it steadies you.

Humility is not low self-esteem. Low self-esteem means you think poorly of yourself and doubt your worth. Humility is the opposite of that — it requires enough self-awareness to see yourself clearly. You can have high self-esteem and still be humble.

Humility is not false modesty. If you are a skilled pianist and someone compliments your playing, saying "Oh no, I'm terrible, I'm nothing special" when you know you're good — that is not humility. That is false modesty, which is actually a form of dishonesty. A truly humble person would say something like "Thank you, I've worked very hard at it." They accept truth without either boasting or denying it.

Humility is not humiliation. Humiliation is something painful that happens to you, often caused by someone else, that makes you feel ashamed or small. Humility, on the other hand, is something that comes from within you. It is quiet and dignified, not painful or shameful.

Once you understand what humility is at its core, you start to see it in several important areas of life:

In how you see yourself. A humble person doesn't constantly need to prove that they are the smartest, the best, or the most important person in the room. They are comfortable without being the center of attention. Their sense of worth doesn't depend on others constantly admiring them.

In how you treat others. Because a humble person doesn't see themselves as superior, they treat others with genuine respect — whether that person is a CEO or a janitor. They listen when others speak. They don't dismiss other people's ideas just because they came from someone "less important."

In how you handle mistakes. A humble person can say "I was wrong" without falling apart, because their identity is not built on being perfect or always right. Admitting a mistake, apologizing sincerely, or asking for help — none of these feel threatening to a humble person. They feel natural.

In how you approach knowledge. This is sometimes called intellectual humility, and it means being open to the possibility that your beliefs, opinions, or understanding could be incomplete or mistaken. A humble person says "I might be wrong about this" or "I don't know — tell me more." They are genuinely curious and open to learning, because they don't assume they already have all the answers.

In how you handle success. When a humble person achieves something, they tend to acknowledge the role that others played — teammates, teachers, circumstances, luck. They don't pretend that every success was entirely their own doing. This doesn't mean they deny their effort or talent; it just means they see the bigger picture.
A Thought That Captures It Beautifully

The writer C.S. Lewis once expressed the idea that humility is not about thinking less of yourself — it is about thinking of yourself less. This is a powerful distinction. A humble person isn't constantly beating themselves up or putting themselves down. They just aren't constantly thinking about themselves at all. Their attention is directed outward — toward others, toward the task at hand, toward what is true — rather than being endlessly focused inward on how they appear or how great they are.

The clearest opposites of humility are arrogance and pride (in its negative sense).

An arrogant person overestimates their own importance, knowledge, and ability. They talk more than they listen. They find it hard to admit mistakes. They dismiss others easily. They tend to believe the rules don't quite apply to them. This kind of excessive pride is essentially the absence of humility.

Humility is not just a nice personality trait — it has real, practical effects on life.

It makes you a better learner, because you're always open to new information rather than assuming you already know. It makes you a better friend, partner, and colleague, because people feel genuinely heard and respected around you. It makes you a better decision-maker, because you seek out different perspectives rather than only trusting your own. And perhaps most importantly, it makes you more trustworthy — people instinctively respect and trust humble people far more than arrogant ones.

Here are some natural examples of how the word humility is used in sentences:

  • "It takes real humility to admit that you've been wrong for years."
  • "Her humility was striking — despite being world-famous, she treated everyone with equal warmth."
  • "The best leaders I've met combine great confidence with deep humility."
  • "He showed humility by asking for feedback instead of assuming his work was perfect."

Humility is the quiet, grounded quality of seeing yourself accurately — neither too big nor too small — which naturally leads you to remain open, respectful, teachable, and honest throughout your life.
8005:
A hummock is a small, rounded mound or bump that rises above the flat or low-lying ground around it. Think of it as a gentle, dome-shaped lump in the landscape — not a mountain, not even a proper hill, but a noticeable little rise that interrupts an otherwise flat surface.

If you imagine a large, flat field with a smooth, rounded lump of earth sticking up from it — like a giant upside-down bowl made of dirt and grass — that's a hummock.
What makes something a hummock, exactly?

Three qualities define it:

  • Small. A hummock is modest in size. You can typically walk around it in seconds or step on top of it without any real effort. It is much smaller than a hill and incomparably smaller than a mountain.
  • Rounded. The top is smooth and dome-like, not jagged, sharp, or flat. Think of a soft curve, not a cliff or a plateau.
  • It stands out from the surrounding ground. A hummock gets its identity from contrast — it rises above the flat or waterlogged terrain around it. Without that surrounding flatness, it wouldn't even be called a hummock; it would just blend into ordinary hilly ground.
The word "hummock" shows up in a few different landscapes, and understanding each one will sharpen your feel for the word:
The simplest case — a small, gentle mound of earth in a meadow, field, or prairie. It's just a little natural bump in the ground.

This is where you'll encounter the word very often. In waterlogged land, the ground is mostly wet and soft, but here and there, small mounds of earth, peat, or thick grass rise above the water. These are hummocks. They matter practically: a person crossing a swamp might jump from hummock to hummock to keep their feet dry, using each little mound as a stepping stone. The ground between hummocks is muddy water; the hummocks themselves are the only solid footing.

In very cold regions, the ground repeatedly freezes and thaws with the seasons. Over time, this process pushes the soil upward into countless small, rounded mounds scattered across the landscape. These are tundra hummocks, and they can make walking across the Arctic extremely tiring — you're constantly stepping up onto a mound and down into the wet hollow beside it, over and over, for miles.

In frozen polar oceans, sheets of ice crash into each other, get pushed upward, and pile up. The rounded, irregular mounds of ice this creates are also called hummocks. Arctic explorers walking across sea ice would have to climb over and around these icy hummocks constantly.
How it differs from similar words

• Hill / Hillock — A hillock is also a small hill, but it implies something made of solid earth, more permanent and more clearly "hill-shaped." A hummock is softer, lower, and often made of ice, peat, or vegetation — not necessarily bare rock and earth.
  • Mound — "Mound" can suggest something man-made (a burial mound, a pitcher's mound). "Hummock" is always natural.
  • Tussock — A tussock is specifically a clump of tall grass that forms a little mound. A tussock can be a type of hummock, but hummock is the broader word — it doesn't have to involve grass at all.
  • Bump — "Bump" is informal and vague. "Hummock" is the precise geographical term for this kind of small, rounded natural rise.

"Hummock" has a slightly rugged, outdoors feel to it. You'll encounter it most in nature writing, geography, ecology, and literature set in wild or cold landscapes — Arctic expeditions, bog crossings, prairie descriptions. It's not a word for cities or manicured parks. It belongs to raw, natural terrain.

• She crossed the bog by leaping from hummock to hummock, trying not to sink into the dark water between them.
  • The tundra was covered in thousands of small hummocks, making every step uneven and exhausting.
  • From a distance, the flat prairie was broken only by a lone hummock near the stream.
  • The expedition report described the sea ice as a jumbled maze of hummocks and pressure ridges.

In short: A hummock is a small, rounded, natural mound — a gentle dome-shaped bump rising above flat or marshy ground. It can be made of earth, ice, peat, or dense vegetation. The word lives in the world of wild landscapes, particularly cold or wet ones.
8006: Hummus is a smooth, creamy food paste — made primarily from chickpeas — that is eaten as a dip or a spread.
What exactly is it made of?

Hummus is built on a small set of core ingredients:

  • Chickpeas (also called garbanzo beans) — small, round, pale-yellow legumes. These are the star ingredient. They are cooked until very soft, then blended into a paste.
  • Tahini — a thick paste made from ground sesame seeds. It adds a slightly nutty, rich flavour.
  • Lemon juice — adds brightness and a mild sourness that balances the richness.
  • Garlic — used in small amounts, it adds depth.
  • Salt — for seasoning.
  • Olive oil — often drizzled on top when serving, adding smoothness and flavour.

All of these are blended together (usually in a food processor or blender) until the mixture becomes silky and smooth.
What does it look, feel, and taste like?

Hummus is soft, thick, and creamy — similar in texture to a very smooth peanut butter or a thick yoghurt. It holds its shape but is easy to scoop.

In colour, it is off-white to pale beige, sometimes with a golden tinge from the olive oil drizzled on top. It is often garnished with a dusting of red paprika or cumin powder, a handful of whole chickpeas, or a sprig of parsley — this makes it look more vibrant and appealing.

The taste is earthy, savoury, and mildly nutty, with a gentle tang from the lemon. It is not spicy on its own, though spicy versions exist.

Hummus is extremely versatile. Here are its most common uses:

  1. As a dip — the most traditional way. You tear off a piece of warm, soft pita bread (a type of Middle Eastern flatbread) and scoop up hummus with it. It is also dipped into with raw vegetables like carrot sticks, cucumber slices, or celery.
  2. As a spread — smeared onto bread, wraps, sandwiches, or toast in place of butter or mayonnaise. It adds flavour and a creamy texture.
  3. As a side dish — served alongside grilled meats, falafel (fried chickpea balls), or other dishes in a full meal.
  4. As a base — sometimes used as the bottom layer of a dish, topped with spiced meat, roasted vegetables, or other toppings.

Hummus is a staple food of the Middle East and the Mediterranean region. It has been eaten for centuries in countries like Lebanon, Israel, Palestine, Egypt, Turkey, Greece, and Syria. It is deeply embedded in the food cultures of these regions — almost every household and restaurant serves it.

Today, hummus is popular worldwide. You will find it in supermarkets, cafés, and restaurants almost everywhere. It has become a mainstream health food globally because it is considered nutritious and satisfying.

Yes, hummus is widely considered a nutritious food. Chickpeas are rich in plant-based protein and dietary fibre, which helps keep you full. Tahini and olive oil provide healthy fats. It is naturally free of added sugar and is suitable for vegetarians and vegans. Because it is filling, flavourful, and made of wholesome ingredients, it is often recommended as a healthy snack or addition to meals.

While the classic version described above is the most common, hummus comes in many variations:

  • Roasted red pepper hummus — blended with roasted red capsicums for a sweeter, slightly smoky taste and a reddish colour.
  • Roasted garlic hummus — uses more garlic, roasted to bring out a sweeter, milder garlic flavour.
  • Spicy hummus — includes chilli or harissa (a spicy North African paste).
  • Black bean hummus — a Western variation that substitutes black beans for chickpeas, giving it a darker colour.
  • Avocado hummus — blended with avocado for a greener, creamier version.

The word "hummus" is sometimes used loosely to refer to any of these blended, dip-like variations, though purists would say only the original chickpea-based version is true hummus.

If you had to remember one sentence: Hummus is a smooth, creamy dip or spread made by blending cooked chickpeas with tahini, lemon juice, garlic, and olive oil — a beloved staple of Middle Eastern cooking, eaten with bread, vegetables, or as part of a larger meal.
8007:
Humongous means extremely large — so large that it stands out, surprises you, or even feels hard to believe. It doesn't just mean "big" or even "very big." It means something is so massive in size, amount, or scale that it almost feels exaggerated or overwhelming.

Think of it as the feeling you get when you see something and your immediate reaction is "Whoa, that is HUGE." That feeling of shock or amazement at the sheer size of something — that is exactly the spirit of this word.
The Crucial Detail: It Is an Informal Word

This is one of the most important things to know. Humongous is a casual, informal word. It belongs to everyday conversation, not to formal or professional writing.

You would say it to a friend. You would not write it in a school essay, a business report, a legal document, or a news article. In those contexts, you would instead use formal alternatives like enormous, immense, or substantial.

So the rule is simple:

  • Casual conversation or informal writing → humongous is perfectly fine.
  • Formal writing or professional settings → choose a more formal word.
What Kind of "Large" Does It Describe?

Humongous is flexible. It can describe the size of almost anything — not just physical objects. Here are the different types of "large" it can express:

Physical size: A humongous building, a humongous elephant, a humongous pizza.

Amount or quantity: A humongous pile of laundry, a humongous sum of money, a humongous crowd.

Degree or scale (abstract things): A humongous mistake, a humongous problem, a humongous opportunity.

In all these cases, the word is pointing at something and saying: this is far, far bigger than you'd normally expect.
How It Sits Among Similar Words

English has many words that mean "large," and they form a kind of scale. Understanding where humongous sits on that scale sharpens your grasp of it.

  • Big → simply larger than average.
  • Large → noticeably bigger than usual.
  • Huge → significantly large; hard to miss.
  • Enormous → impressively and strikingly large.
  • Gigantic / Colossal → extremely large, almost beyond normal scale.
  • Humongous → sits right alongside gigantic and colossal in terms of sheer size, but with an added sense of informality and expressive emphasis. It carries more personality and drama than the others.

The key difference between humongous and words like enormous or colossal is not just size — it is tone. Humongous sounds lively, vivid, and conversational. The other words sound neutral and composed. When you use humongous, you are not just describing size — you are expressing a reaction to it.
The Emotional Color of the Word

Humongous is not a neutral, cold description. It carries energy. When someone says something is humongous, they are almost always expressing:

  • Surprise — "I didn't expect it to be this big."
  • Admiration — "This is impressively large."
  • Playful exaggeration — "This is so big it's almost ridiculous."

Because of this emotional warmth, the word is also widely used with children, in playful contexts, in storytelling, and whenever someone wants to sound expressive rather than clinical.

Here are examples that show the word doing different jobs:

  1. "That's a humongous watermelon — how are we going to carry it?"

(Physical size, casual surprise)

  1. "They made a humongous mistake by not reading the contract."

(Abstract — the scale of an error)

  1. "There was a humongous crowd at the concert. I could barely see the stage."

(Quantity of people)

  1. "She felt a humongous sense of relief after finishing her exams."

(Emotional scale — how large a feeling was)

  1. "The company spent a humongous amount of money on advertising last year."

(Quantity of money, informal business talk)

Notice how in each case, the speaker is not just stating a fact — they are reacting with a kind of emphasis, almost pointing at the thing and widening their eyes at it.

Since the word is informal, there are clear situations where it is the wrong choice:

  • Formal essays or academic writing: Avoid it. Use enormous, substantial, significant, or considerable.
  • Professional emails to senior colleagues or clients: Better to use neutral, formal language.
  • News reporting or journalism: Not appropriate.
  • Legal or scientific writing: Never.

But in a text message, a casual blog post, a conversation, a children's story, or creative fiction where the narrator has a vivid voice — humongous fits perfectly.
The One-Sentence Definition You'll Never Forget

If you had to boil it all down: humongous means extremely large, used in informal contexts, and carries a sense of expressive surprise or emphasis at how big something is.

That's the whole word. Everything else is just detail layered on top of that core.
8008:
Humor refers to the quality in something that makes it funny, amusing, or capable of making people laugh or smile. It also refers to a person's ability to notice, enjoy, and express that funniness.

Think of it in two directions:

  • Humor in a thing: "There was real humor in the situation." (The situation had a funny quality to it.)
  • Humor in a person: "She has a great sense of humor." (She notices and appreciates what's funny.)

Both directions are the same word, just applied differently — one is about where the funniness lives, the other is about who can see and feel it.

1. Humor as a Quality (in situations, stories, or speech)

When we say something "has humor" or "contains humor," we mean it holds a quality that triggers amusement in people. This quality usually comes from surprise, absurdity, irony, clever wordplay, timing, or a gap between what we expect and what actually happens.

For example, a story where a serious professor slips on a banana peel has humor in it — the contrast between dignity and clumsiness is the source of the funniness. The humor doesn't lie in the banana peel alone; it lies in the relationship between the professor's seriousness and the ridiculous outcome.

This is why humor is often described as being "found" in things — it's a hidden property that someone can either spot or miss.

2. Sense of Humor (in a person)

A person's sense of humor is their inner ability to recognize what's funny and to enjoy it. It is deeply personal — different people find different things amusing, which is why we say people have different senses of humor.

Someone with a sharp sense of humor catches subtle jokes quickly. Someone with a broad sense of humor laughs at many different types of things. Someone with no sense of humor (or a poor one) struggles to see the funny side of things — they take everything literally or seriously.

You can also have humor as a personality trait, meaning you naturally produce amusement in others — you say funny things, see life comically, and bring lightness to situations.

3. Humor as a Mood or State of Mind

In a slightly more formal or old-fashioned usage, humor means a person's current mood or mental state. This is why we say:

  • "She was in good humor today" — she was in a pleasant, cheerful mood.
  • "He replied out of humor" — he replied while in a bad or irritable mood.
  • "The crowd was in ill humor" — the crowd was displeased or upset.

This usage is less common in everyday modern speech, but you'll still encounter it in literature, formal writing, and certain expressions. When you do, just remember it simply means mood or disposition.

4. The Historical Meaning (Important Background)

For hundreds of years, the word "humor" referred to one of the four bodily fluids that ancient and medieval doctors believed controlled human health and personality. These were blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile. Doctors believed your personality and mood were determined by which of these fluids dominated your body.

This is actually why humor came to mean mood — it was literally thought to flow through your body and shape how you felt. And gradually, over centuries, it evolved further to mean the lightness and amusement we associate with the word today.

You don't need to use this meaning in modern life, but knowing it helps you understand why "humor" and "mood" are connected, and why you'll see this medical usage in older texts, Shakespeare, and historical writing.

Humor is not one single thing — it comes in many forms, and knowing them helps you understand the word more fully.

Dry humor (also called deadpan): The joke is delivered with a completely straight face and no obvious attempt to be funny. The humor comes from the contrast between the seriousness of the delivery and the absurdity of what's being said.

Dark humor: Jokes about death, suffering, tragedy, or uncomfortable subjects. It makes light of things that are usually considered serious or taboo. Some people find this liberating; others find it offensive.

Self-deprecating humor: Making jokes at your own expense — laughing at your own flaws, mistakes, or embarrassments. It tends to make a person seem humble and likable.

Sarcastic humor: Saying the opposite of what you mean, usually with a sharp or mocking tone. "Oh great, another Monday. My absolute favorite."

Absurdist humor: Humor based on things that are deliberately illogical, random, or surreal. The joke doesn't need to make rational sense — the nonsense is the point.

Observational humor: Pointing out funny truths about everyday life that people recognize immediately — "Why do we say we're going to 'get some sleep' as if sleep might not be there?"

Physical humor (slapstick): Humor based on exaggerated physical actions — falls, collisions, silly faces, exaggerated reactions.

These aren't rigid categories. Real humor often blends several of these at once.

This is one of the most fascinating things about the word — humor is felt, not just described. Scholars, philosophers, and psychologists have long tried to explain why things are funny. A few widely accepted ideas:

Incongruity: Something is funny when two things that don't belong together are suddenly paired. A dog wearing glasses and reading a newspaper is funny because dogs and reading glasses are wildly mismatched.

Surprise: Jokes work by leading you in one direction and then suddenly turning. The setup creates an expectation; the punchline breaks it. Your brain's reaction to that sudden shift feels like amusement.

Relief: Some humor releases tension — you laugh because the anxiety built up and then suddenly dissolved.

Superiority: Some humor involves laughing at someone else's misfortune or foolishness, giving the audience a brief feeling of being "above" the situation.

Most jokes and comedic situations use at least one of these mechanisms.

These words are often confused, so it helps to understand how they differ:

Humor is the broadest term — it refers to the general quality or capacity for funniness. It's warm, relatable, and often gentle.

Wit is sharper and more intellectual. It's humor that comes from clever, quick thinking and smart wordplay. Wit impresses; humor endears.

Comedy is usually the structured or performative form — stand-up comedy, a comedy film, a comedic play. It's humor presented as an art or craft.

Joke is a specific unit — a single funny thing said or written, with a clear setup and punchline. Humor is the larger quality; a joke is one expression of it.

Amusement is what you feel as a result of humor — the pleasant, light feeling of being entertained or tickled.
Common Phrases and How to Use Them

• "Sense of humor" — a person's ability to find or appreciate what's funny. ("You need a sense of humor to work here.")
  • "In good humor" — in a pleasant, cheerful mood. ("The boss was in good humor after the meeting.")
  • "Out of humor" — in a bad or irritable mood. ("He was out of humor all morning.")
  • "Humor in the situation" — a funny quality within something that happened. ("There was some humor in the fact that the fire drill happened exactly when the food arrived.")
  • "Dark humor" — jokes about grim or uncomfortable subjects.
  • "Dry humor" — understated, straight-faced funniness.
  • "A touch of humor" — a small, light amount of funniness in something. ("Her speech had just a touch of humor to lighten the mood.")
The Deeper Significance of the Word

Humor is considered a deeply human quality. The ability to laugh at life — especially its painful, awkward, or absurd parts — is seen across all cultures as a coping mechanism, a social bonding tool, and a sign of emotional intelligence. People who can bring humor into difficult situations are often admired for their resilience.

This is why the word carries warmth. Saying someone "has humor" or "has a good sense of humor" is almost always a compliment — it suggests they are self-aware, socially skilled, and pleasant to be around.

Humor also builds trust and connection between people. Shared laughter is one of the fastest ways humans bond with each other, which is why humor is central to friendship, storytelling, public speaking, and even difficult conversations.

MeaningExample

In short: humor as a noun means the quality that makes something funny, a person's ability to appreciate or create funniness, or (more formally) a person's mood. It can live in a story, a situation, a person, or a piece of writing. It comes in many styles — dry, dark, absurdist, sarcastic, and more. It works through surprise, incongruity, and the subversion of expectations. And it is considered one of the most valued and humanizing qualities a person can possess.
8009:
To humor someone means to go along with what they want, say, or believe — even if you don't fully agree with it — just to keep them happy or avoid trouble.

You are not necessarily doing it because you think they're right. You're doing it because it feels easier, kinder, or more practical than pushing back.

When you humor someone, there's a quiet understanding inside you: "I don't quite agree with this, but I'll play along."

This is what makes the word special. It carries the idea of patient tolerance or gentle indulgence. You are, in a sense, accommodating the other person's feelings, wishes, or quirks — choosing peace over argument, or kindness over correction.

Think of it like this: a parent knows Santa Claus isn't real, but when their five-year-old insists on leaving cookies out, the parent plays along and eats those cookies the next morning. The parent is humoring the child.

People humor others for a few common reasons:

  • To avoid conflict. It's not worth arguing about.
  • To be kind. Correcting the person might hurt their feelings.
  • To manage a difficult person. Pushing back might make things worse.
  • To show patience. You respect that they feel strongly about something.
  • To just get through a moment. It's easier to go along right now.

You often see it happen when:

  • Someone has an unusual or stubborn belief
  • Someone makes a repeated request that you find a little unnecessary
  • Someone is in a fragile emotional state
  • Someone is being demanding or unreasonable and you choose tolerance

Example 1
Your friend believes a certain route is faster, even though you know from experience it's not. You take their route anyway without arguing. You humored them.

Example 2
Your grandmother tells the same story every Sunday about how she once met a famous singer. You listen each time with a smile, even though you've heard it twenty times. You are humoring her.

Example 3
Your manager has an idea that you privately think is weak, but you don't challenge it in the meeting. You go along with it. You humored your manager.

Example 4
Someone at work is having a rough day and says, "I think the whole world is against me." You don't argue. You just say, "I understand." You're humoring them a little — not correcting their dramatic statement, but letting them feel heard.
The Very Common Phrase: "Just Humor Me"

This phrase is used when the speaker is asking you to go along with something, often knowing you might be doubtful or unwilling.

  • "I know it sounds strange, but just humor me and try it once."
  • "Humor me — let's check the map one more time just to be sure."
  • "I know you think it's a silly idea, but humor me."

When someone says "just humor me," they're essentially saying: "Please play along, even if you're skeptical. Do this for me."

This is important, because the word is easy to confuse with similar ideas:

It's not the same as agreeing.
When you agree with someone, you genuinely share their view. When you humor someone, you may privately disagree — but you go along anyway.

It's not the same as obeying.
Obeying is about following an order or rule, often with no choice. Humoring is voluntary, softer, and often done out of kindness or convenience.

It's not the same as lying.
You're not deceiving someone with false information. You're simply choosing not to challenge or correct them in that moment.

It's not the same as supporting.
Supporting someone means you genuinely back them. Humoring someone means you're just not getting in their way.

The word can carry a slightly different feel depending on the context:

  • Warm and affectionate: Humoring an elderly relative or a child — this feels loving and patient.
  • Slightly condescending: If you humor someone because you privately think they're being foolish or naive, there can be a faint air of "I know better, but I'll let this go."
  • Neutral and practical: Sometimes you just humor someone to get through a situation efficiently, with no emotional charge at all.

None of these are wrong. The tone depends entirely on context and intention.
The Full Picture in One Sentence

To humor someone is to willingly go along with their wishes, beliefs, or behavior — not because you fully agree, but as an act of patience, kindness, or practicality — to keep the peace or make them feel comfortable.
